cells.tense: You are standing at the threshold right now, and you know what you are carrying across it.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're carrying into the next room and one thing you're leaving on the table.
cells.core: You can hold what you came from and what you're walking toward in the same hand. You've stopped arguing with the leaving, and that's why it's not taking anything from you. When a shared thing reaches its edge, you feel it and you keep moving — no drama, no dragging it along.\n\nWhat that looks like going well is plain. You tell people what matters before the goodbye. You say the true thing at the table instead of saving it for a later that doesn't come. Your mind is quiet enough to do that, and the quiet is doing the work — you trust the read you get about when a thing is finished, and you act on it while the people in it can still hear you.
cells.sheetLine: You can leave without abandoning and arrive without erasing.
cells.place: the open moment before any possibility has been chosen

cells.tense: You will have already crossed and left before anyone has noticed you were in the room.
cells.ask: Stay in the next conversation five minutes longer than feels finished and say one thing you'd normally leave out.
cells.core: You're racing the threshold. Somewhere ahead you've already decided the connection is over, and you're living in that ending before it arrives — measuring every exchange against a departure that hasn't happened. The bracing is what makes it feel inevitable.\n\nThe work waiting for you is the building that comes after a clean ending, and you can't build while you're rehearsing the exit. The room you're in is real; the one you're packing for is not. When a goodbye is handled well here, you stay for the whole conversation, you let the last thing be said out loud, and the next thing starts from ground instead of from air. Five more minutes is usually where that lives.
cells.sheetLine: You're packing for a departure nobody has announced.

cells.tense: You were standing at a threshold you already walked through, and you still describe yourself as being on the far side.
cells.ask: Write down one pattern about how you leave rooms and test it against something that actually happened this month.
cells.core: Something in what you shared stopped being shared a while back, and you're still narrating it as present — still at the edge, still deciding. The decision happened. What hasn't happened is you looking at the pattern plainly: how you arrive, how you go quiet, what you actually do when a connection starts to change.\n\nPutting one of those patterns on paper and checking it against a real month gives you your footing back without forcing feeling into a place that's run empty. When this is working, you notice a thing is over while it's still going, and you say so to the people in it — not often after, not in a letter you don't send. Seeing the shape is the whole of it; the timing follows.
cells.sheetLine: The crossing already happened. You're narrating the wrong side.

cells.tense: You are already the one setting the terms of what carries forward, and you talk about it as if the terms set themselves.
cells.ask: Catch one moment this week where you decide what gets kept and say to yourself, plainly, that you chose it.
cells.core: You're the one who decides what survives the crossing. What gets remembered, what gets taught, what gets let go — those calls are yours, and when you make them well, people around you end up carrying the same things you carry. It works because you're good at it, not because a current is doing it.\n\nThe trouble is in how you tell it. You describe those calls as just how things are, and the doing goes unattributed — nobody hears that a person did it, including you. When this is whole, you can point at a thing you kept and say, without flinching, that you kept it. One moment is enough to start; the phrase is short and it can be said quietly.
cells.sheetLine: You're the one keeping it. Say so, once, to yourself.
cells.place: the open moment before any possibility has been chosen
